Jones Jr.''' (May 25, 1932 – December 25, 2020) was an American professional [[basketball]] player and coach. He is best known for his association with the [[Boston Celtics]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA), with whom he won 11 of his 12 [[NBA championship]]s (eight as a player, two as an assistant coach, and two as a head coach).{{Cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/history/legends/kc-jones/index.html|title=NBA Legends profile: K.C. Jones|website=[[NBA.com]] }} As a player, he is tied for third for [[List of NBA players with most championships|most NBA championships]] in a career, and is one of three NBA players with an unsurpassed 8–0 record in NBA Finals series.{{citation |last=Berkman |first=Seth |title=N.B.A. Finals Legend or Loser? Luck Is Often the Difference | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 19, 2016 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/20/sports/basketball/lebron-james-nba-finals-legend-or-loser-luck-is-often-the-difference.html}} He is the only African-American coach other than [[Bill Russell]] to have won multiple NBA championships,{{Cite web|url=https://www.latestnewssouthafrica.com/2020/12/25/legendary-celtics-player-coach-k-c-jones-dies-at-the-of-88/|title=K.C. Jones death & cause of death - What killed Legendary Celtics player, coach K.C. Jones, Age & Obituary|date=December 25, 2020}}{{Cite web|url=http://thestartingfive.net/2008/02/14/throwback-thursday-kc-jones/|title=Throwback Thursday: K.C. Jones|date=February 14, 2008|website=The Starting Five|access-date=June 20, 2017|archive-date=August 10, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810221319/http://thestartingfive.net/2008/02/14/throwback-thursday-kc-jones/|url-status=dead}} and one of eight players to ever achieve the [[Triple Crown (American basketball)|basketball Triple Crown]]. Jones was inducted into the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] in 1989. ==Early life== Jones was born in [[Taylor, Texas]], as the oldest of six children. The initials "K.C." were his given name; he inherited the same name as his father, a factory worker and cook, who himself was named after the fabled railroad engineer [[Casey Jones]].{{cite news |last1=Myhre |first1=Rich |title=Pulled muscle lands Dailey on injury list |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-herald-pulled-muscle-lands-dai/169359044/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=The Daily Herald |date=January 10, 1991 |page=15 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} When Jones was aged nine, his parents divorced and he moved to [[San Francisco]], California, with his mother and two siblings.{{cite web |title=Jones, K. C. |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/jones-k-c |website=Encyclopedia.com |access-date=December 29, 2020 |date=December 21, 2020}} He learned to play basketball on a patch of gravel. Jones attended Commerce High School in San Francisco where he played basketball and [[American football|football]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.nba.com/history/legends/profiles/kc-jones|title=Legends profile: K.C. Jones|website=NBA.com}} He considered himself to be a better football player than a basketball player in high school.{{cite news |last1=Stiles |first1=Maxwell |title=Styles in Sports |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/los-angeles-mirror-styles-in-sports/169274780/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=Los Angeles Mirror |date=July 28, 1958 |page=24 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} ==College career== Jones played [[college basketball]] at the [[University of San Francisco]] and, along with [[Bill Russell]], guided the [[San Francisco Dons men's basketball|Dons]] to [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] championships in 1955 and 1956.{{Cite web|date=December 25, 2020|title=USF Hoops Legend K.C. Jones Dies; Led Dons With Bill Russell To Back-To-Back NCAA Titles|url=https://sanfrancisco.cbslocal.com/2020/12/25/usf-hoops-legend-k-c-jones-dies-led-dons-with-bill-russell-to-back-to-back-ncaa-titles/|access-date=December 26, 2020|language=en-US}} During their time with the Dons, Russell and Jones led the team to a then-record 55-game win streak{{cite web| last = Schneider| first = Bernie| title = 1953–56 NCAA Championship Seasons: The Bill Russell Years|publisher= University of San Francisco| url= http://usfdons.cstv.com/trads/russell_years.html| year = 2006| access-date = December 1, 2006| archive-url = https://archive.today/20061128191756/http://usfdons.cstv.com/trads/russell_years.html| archive-date = November 28, 2006}} (including an undefeated 29–0 record during the [[1955–56 NCAA men's basketball season|1955–56 season]]) and helped pioneer a play that later became known as the [[Alley-oop (basketball)|alley-oop]].{{Cite book| last = Johnson | first = James W. | title = The Dandy Dons: Bill Russell, K. C. Jones, Phil Woolpert, and One of College Basketball's Greatest and Most Innovative Teams| publisher = Bison Books | year = 2009 | page = 85 | isbn = 9780803224445}}{{cite web | last = Paul | first = Alan | title=An Interview With Bill Russell|url=http://alanpaul.net/2018/04/an-interview-with-bill-russell/| year=2018}} Jones also played with Russell on [[1956 United States men's Olympic basketball team|the United States national team]] which won the gold medal at the [[Basketball at the 1956 Summer Olympics|1956 Olympic Games]] in [[Melbourne]], Australia, while defeating their opponents by an unsurpassed average margin of 53.5 points per game.{{Cite web|date=December 26, 2020|title=Melbourne 1956 Olympic champion and basketball legend Jones dies at 88|url=https://www.insidethegames.biz/articles/1102417/kc-jones-basketball-melbourne-1956|access-date=December 26, 2020|website=insidethegames.biz}} Jones served two years in the [[United States Army]] from 1956 to 1958. In July 1958, Jones tried out for the [[Los Angeles Rams]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL); the Rams had drafted him in the 30th round of the [[1955 NFL draft]]. He decided to try for a football career because he did not know if he had the ability to make it as a professional basketball player.{{cite news |title=Rams Using K. C. Jones |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/syracuse-herald-journal-rams-using-k-c/169275178/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=Syracuse Herald-Journal |date=August 10, 1958 |page=5 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} Jones had not played a full season of football since his senior year at Commerce High School and only played in one regulation game afterwards during his stint in the army. Jones planned to report to the Boston Celtics in September if he failed to make the Rams. Playing as a defensive [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]], he was considered a likely candidate to make the team after preseason performances against the [[Washington Redskins]] and [[New York Giants]].{{cite news |last1=Whorton |first1=Cal |title=K. C. Jones Quits Rams for Bid With Celtic Pro Cagers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-k-c-jones-quits/169275029/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=September 3, 1958 |page=57 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} On September 2, 1958, Jones decided that he wanted to play for the Celtics and left the Rams. ==Professional career== ===Boston Celtics (1958–1967)=== [[File:Kc jones cropped.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Jones with the Boston Celtics in 1964]] During his playing days, he was known as a tenacious defender. Jones spent all of his nine seasons in the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] with the [[Boston Celtics]], being part of [[List of NBA players with most championships|eight championship teams]] from 1959 to 1966, retiring after the Celtics' loss to the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] in the 1967 Eastern Division finals. He was inducted into the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] in 1989.{{Cite web|url=https://www.timesreporter.com/sports/20171119/bump-and-run--or-just-boxing-out-kc-jones-left-impact-on-nfl|title=Bump and run ... or just boxing out? K.C. Jones left impact on NFL|first=Jon|last=Kendle|website=Times Reporter|access-date=March 17, 2019|archive-date=September 22, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200922051533/https://www.timesreporter.com/sports/20171119/bump-and-run--or-just-boxing-out-kc-jones-left-impact-on-nfl|url-status=dead}} Jones is one of only eight players in basketball history to achieve the [[Triple Crown (American basketball)|basketball Triple Crown]] — winning an NCAA championship, an NBA championship, and an Olympic gold medal,{{Cite web|url=http://www.thepostgame.com/blog/list/201207/basketball-triple-crown-ncaa-nba-championships-olympic-gold-medal|title=Basketball's Exclusive Triple Crown Club|date=December 31, 1969|website=ThePostGame.com|access-date=April 21, 2015|archive-date=February 12, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212194202/http://www.thepostgame.com/blog/list/201207/basketball-triple-crown-ncaa-nba-championships-olympic-gold-medal|url-status=dead}}{{cite news |last=Beslic |first= Stephen|date=November 11, 2022 |title=Eight players who have won NCAA, NBA, and Olympic titles |url=https://www.basketballnetwork.net/latest-news/seven-players-who-have-won-ncaa-nba-and-olympic-titles |work= Basketball Network|location= |access-date=November 27, 2024}}{{cite news |last= Cohn|first=Jordan |date= October 11, 2020|title= Anthony Davis joins 7 other players to win NBA Finals, NCAA Championship, Olympic gold medal|url=https://www.audacy.com/thefandc/sports/nba/anthony-davis-joins-basketballs-triple-crown-club |work=[[106.7 The Fan]] |location= |access-date=November 27, 2024}} joining [[Bill Russell]], [[Magic Johnson]], [[Michael Jordan]], [[Jerry Lucas]], [[Clyde Lovellette]], [[Quinn Buckner]], and [[Anthony Davis]]. In NBA history, only his former teammates Russell (11 championships) and [[Sam Jones (basketball, born 1933)|Sam Jones]] (10) have won more championships during their playing careers.{{Cite web|title=Celtics legend K.C. Jones dies at 88|url=https://www.nba.com/news/celtics-legend-k-c-jones-dies-at-88|access-date=December 26, 2020|website=NBA.com}} ===Hartford Capitols (1967–1968)=== On September 11, 1967, Jones announced that he would play for the [[Hartford Capitols]] of the [[Eastern Professional Basketball League]] (EPBL).{{cite news |title=K.C. Jones to play for EBL five |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-morning-news-kc-jones-to-play-for/204986569/ |access-date=August 31, 2026 |work=The Morning News |date=September 12, 1967 |page=21 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} He joined the Capitols because his coaching job at [[Brandeis University]] meant he was based nearby and he would be able to play on weekends. On November 12, Jones scored 5 points in his debut against the Wilmington Blue Bombers.{{cite news |last1=Canfield |first1=Owen |title=Caps Capture 134-118 Win From Bombers In Home Opener |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/hartford-courant-caps-capture-134-118-wi/204986577/ |access-date=August 31, 2026 |work=Hartford Courant |date=November 13, 1967 |page=45 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} He appeared in a total of 6 games with an average of 6.5 points, 4.0 rebounds and 6.8 assists per game.{{cite web |title=K.C. Jones minor league basketball statistics |url=https://www.statscrew.com/minorbasketball/stats/p-joneskc001 |website=Stats Crew |access-date=August 31, 2026}} On January 5, 1968, Jones was placed on the Capitols' [[Practice squad|taxi squad]] at his own request and was not expected to play again.{{cite news |title=Capitols Place K.C. Jones on Taxi Squad |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/hartford-courant-capitols-place-kc-jon/204986580/ |access-date=August 31, 2026 |work=Hartford Courant |date=January 5, 1968 |page=18 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} He reflected on his Capitols tenure: "I can't shoot, and I didn't feel like I was helping them enough. Nine years a pro and I still can't shoot. It's frustrating. I never was a complete player."{{cite news |last1=Fitzgerald |first1=Ray |title=K.C. Jones at Brandeis: 'I've Got a Lot to Learn' |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/41015549/ |access-date=August 31, 2026 |work=The Boston Globe |date=January 3, 1968 |page=48 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} ==Coaching career== Jones began his coaching career at [[Brandeis University]], serving as its head coach from 1967 to 1970. He served as an assistant coach at [[Harvard University]] from 1970 to 1971.{{Cite web|url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1970/5/1/former-celtic-k-c-jones-to/|title=Former Celtic K. C. Jones To Coach Basketball Here | News | The Harvard Crimson|website=thecrimson.com}} Jones then reunited with former teammate [[Bill Sharman]] as the assistant coach for the 1971–72 NBA champion [[Los Angeles Lakers]]. During that season, the team won a record 33 straight games. He became the first-ever head coach of the [[American Basketball Association|ABA]]'s [[San Diego Conquistadors]] on August 8, 1972.[https://www.nytimes.com/1972/08/09/archives/personalities-k-c-jones-hired.html White Jr., Gordon S. "Personalities: K.C. Jones Hired," ''The New York Times'', Wednesday, August 9, 1972.] Retrieved December 1, 2020 One week after Jones' only season with the Conquistadors ended with his resignation, he returned to the NBA and agreed with the [[Washington Wizards|Baltimore Bullets]], who were in the process of relocating to [[Washington, D.C.]], to take over for [[Gene Shue]] as head coach for the soon-to-be-renamed [[1973–74 Capital Bullets season|Capital Bullets]] on June 18, 1973; the team would add Washington to its name beginning in 1974.[https://www.nytimes.com/1973/06/19/archives/k-c-jones-named-coach-of-nba-s-capital-bullets-jones-to-coach.html Rogers, Thomas. "K. C. Jones Named Coach Of N.B.A.'s Capital Bullets," ''The New York Times'', Tuesday, June 19, 1973.] Retrieved December 1, 2020 During his three years in Washington, the Bullets had a 155–91 win‐loss record and arguably the most talented team in the league. Being swept by the [[Golden State Warriors]] in the [[1975 NBA Finals]] and a seven-game loss to the [[Cleveland Cavaliers]] in the [[1976 NBA playoffs|Eastern Conference semifinals the following year]] resulted in Jones' contract not being renewed on May 7, 1976.[https://www.nytimes.com/1976/05/08/archives/kc-jones-discharged-as-bullets-coach-kc-jones-dismissed-by-bullets.html Goldaper, Sam. "K. C. Jones Discharged as Bullets’ Coach," ''The New York Times'', Saturday, May 8, 1976.] Retrieved December 1, 2020 He was replaced by [[Dick Motta]] three weeks later on May 28, 1976.[https://www.nytimes.com/1976/05/29/archives/motta-to-coach-bullets-76ers-sold-motta-hired-by-bullets-76ers-sold.html Goldaper, Sam. "Motta to Coach Bullets," ''The New York Times'', Saturday, May 29, 1976.] Retrieved December 1, 2020 [[File:K.C. Jones 1984.jpg|thumb|right|Jones as head coach of the [[Boston Celtics]], {{circa}} 1984]] In 1983, Jones took over as head coach of the Boston Celtics, replacing [[Bill Fitch]]. Jones guided the [[Larry Bird]]-led Celtics to championships in 1984 and 1986.{{cite web|last=Twiss|first=Jeff|url=https://www.nba.com/celtics/history/The1984NBAFinals_121203.html|title=The 1984 NBA Finals|work=NBA.com|access-date=February 17, 2020}} Also in 1986, Jones led the Eastern squad in the [[1986 NBA All-Star Game]] in [[Dallas]] at the [[Reunion Arena]], beating the Western squad 139–132. The Celtics won the [[Atlantic Division (NBA)|Atlantic Division]] in all five of Jones's seasons as head coach and reached the NBA Finals in four of his five years as coach. In a surprise announcement, he retired after the 1987–88 season and was succeeded by assistant coach [[Jimmy Rodgers (basketball)|Jimmy Rodgers]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/05/04/sports/k-c-jones-to-retire-as-coach.html|title=K. C. Jones to Retire as Coach (Published 1988)|newspaper=The New York Times|date=May 4, 1988}} Jones spent one season in the Celtics' front office in 1988–89, then resigned to join the [[Seattle SuperSonics]] as an assistant coach and basketball consultant for the 1989–90 season.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/08/16/sports/sports-people-basketball-k-c-jones-leaves-celtics-to-join-sonics.html|title=Sports People: BASKETBALL; K. C. Jones Leaves Celtics to Join Sonics (Published 1989)|newspaper=The New York Times|date=August 16, 1989}} He served as head coach of the Sonics in 1990–91 and 1991–92.{{Cite web|title=Boston Celtics legend K.C. Jones dies at age 88|url=https://www.sportingnews.com/au/nba/news/boston-celtics-legendary-player-and-coach-hall-of-famer-kc-jones-dies-at-88/1fg67ir6zwmtv1ljk9xcdx09v9|access-date=December 26, 2020|website=sportingnews.com|date=December 25, 2020}} In 1994, Jones joined the [[Detroit Pistons]] as an assistant coach for one season. The Pistons' head coach at that time, [[Don Chaney]], had previously played for Jones with the Celtics.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/03/sports/sports-people-basketball-k-c-jones-returns-as-aide-with-pistons.html |title=K. C. Jones Returns as Aide With Pistons |newspaper=The New York Times|date=September 3, 1994|access-date=2013-03-07}} Jones was also considered to once again coach the Celtics during the off-season in 1995.{{Cite web|first=Michael|last=Arace|title=Ford Reaches Point of No Return With Celtics|url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-1995-05-18-9505180302-story.html|website=courant.com|date=May 18, 1995 |access-date=January 1, 2019|archive-date=January 2, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190102051241/https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-1995-05-18-9505180302-story.html|url-status=bot: unknown}} 02 January 2019 In 1996, Jones returned to the Boston Celtics, this time as an assistant coach for one season.{{Cite web|url=https://www.inquirer.com/archives/|title=Archives | The Philadelphia Inquirer|website=inquirer.com}} Jones returned to the professional coaching ranks in 1997, guiding the [[New England Blizzard]] of the fledgling women's [[American Basketball League (1996–1998)|American Basketball League]] (1996–1998) through its last {{frac|1|1|2}} seasons of existence. The Blizzard made the playoffs in his second year as head coach, but they were summarily dispatched by the [[San Jose Lasers]].{{Cite web|last1=Swan|first1=Gary|date=February 23, 1998|title=Lasers Wrap Up Playoff Sweep / Machanguana proves too much for Blizzard|url=https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/Lasers-Wrap-Up-Playoff-Sweep-Machanguana-proves-3310636.php|access-date=December 26, 2020|website=sfgate.com}} ==Personal life== Jones married Beverly Cain – the sister of his Olympic teammate [[Carl Cain]] – in 1959;{{cite web |last1=Kahn |first1=Joseph P. |title=K.C. Jones, a Celtics legend and 12-time NBA champion, dies at 88 |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2020/12/25/metro/kc-jones-celtics-legend-12-time-nba-champion-dies-88/ |website=The Boston Globe |access-date=September 7, 2021 |date=December 25, 2020}} they had five children together before they divorced. He had a sixth child with his second wife, Ellen.{{cite news |last1=DuPree |first1=David |title=Jones: Doubly Sweet Second Time Around |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1983/11/22/jones-doubly-sweet-second-time-around/6b486b35-21ea-4e67-81f5-013163ee7762/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=September 7, 2021 |date=November 22, 1983}} His son, Kipper, played as a guard at [[Bentley College]]. His daughter, Bryna, received a basketball and volleyball scholarship to attend the [[University of Hawaiʻi]].{{cite news |title=K.C. Still Has a Basketball Jones |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1997/07/08/kc-still-has-a-basketball-jones/31f7035d-0838-4668-91f5-cb785d12e345/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=September 7, 2021 |date=July 8, 1997}} ===Death=== Jones died on December 25, 2020, at an assisted living center in Connecticut, aged 88. He had [[Alzheimer's disease]].{{citation |last=Goldstein|first=Richard |title=K.C. Jones, Celtics Standout as Player and Coach, Dies at 88 | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=December 25, 2020 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/25/sports/kc-jones-dead.html?action=click&module=Well&pgtype=Homepage§ion=Obituaries}}{{cite web |title=Legendary Boston Celtics player, coach K.C.
